newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian riot police protect Israeli trade fair.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian riot police protect Israeli trade fair.

text.p: Israel's first trade fair in Jordan went ahead on Wednesday but with a heavy police presence to prevent disruption by about 1,000 angry protesters.

"The (Jordanian) opposition to the exhibition is being used as an excuse to express dissatisfaction with the peace process, Jordan's peace treaty with Israel and even the existence of the state of Israel," Israeli ambassador to Jordan, Shimon Shamir, told reporters at the opening ceremony.

Scores of riot police blocked about 1,000 Jordanian protesters who tried to reach the site of the trade fair hours before it was due to open, witnesses said. Organisers delayed the opening of the exhibition by a few hours.

Three rows of police formed human chains to seal off the main street leading to the fair. They earlier shoved away scores of demonstrators chanting Islam's rallying cry of "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) and "Jordan's land is Arab not Zionist".
Some police officers tore banners and a few protesters were slightly bruised in minor scuffles, witnesses said. An armoured police vehicle splashed coloured water over some protesters.
Laith Shubailat, a vocal opposition activist who heads the Islamist dominated Jordan Engineers Association, attacked the government "for becoming an agent of Zionism to Judaise Jordan."

Former prime minister and intelligence chief Ahmed Obeidat, who led the campaign, urged calm, telling the protesters that "the security forces are brother Jordanians like us...their feelings are like ours and they are only given orders".
"Our aim is the security of Jordan...The insistence of the authorities to allow this exhibition to take place is damaging Jordan's security by allowing Israel to penetrate us," Obeidat told Reuters.
The demonstration was organised by a national committee that represents a broad-based coalition of parties and unions.
The grouping reflects the strength of anti-Israeli feelings among many Jordanians who still shun contacts despite the 1994 peace treaty that ended a 46-year state of war.
The committee accused the government of preventing their supporters in cities across the country from setting off in buses organised to bring demonstrators to Amman.
Seventy Israeli companies have set up stalls on the exhibition's site with over 150 Israeli businessmen attending.
